title: How Could a Router Lead to a Nationwide Ground Stop?
summary: Aviation experts and federal officials said the network outage began after a new piece of networking equipment began flooding the rest of the system with data. The underlying cause is unclear.

Thousands of flights were halted for hours on Friday after officials issued a[rare nationwide ground stop](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-stop-flights-what-to-know.html) , creating a cascade of delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend.


Government officials blamed the disarray on a router in Arkansas that sent a flood of data into the Federal Aviation Administration’s system after an upgrade. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at another complex in Texas.


Officials shut down the airspace out of an abundance of caution as the network became “unpredictable and unreliable,” said Michael McCormick, a professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Daytona Beach, Fla.


“It was a smart decision to actually decide to ground-stop all air departures,” he said.


On Sunday, authorities were still working to determine an exact cause for the communications network failure that prompted officials to issue the ground stop.


Here’s what we know about what could have caused the domino effect at airports.


## What happened on Friday?


Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday that[the cascade of failures began during a routine router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/sean-duffy-ground-stop-trump-faa.html) Workers felt that the station was remote enough to work on without causing undue harm, which turned out not to be the case.


Across the country, the Federal Aviation Administration has slowly been modernizing its antiquated copper-wire-based system to fiber optic cable, which was what workers were upgrading in Arkansas at the time of the network crash.
